i18n.en: After kingship had descended from heaven,

notes.official:
The composition opens with its signature formula *nam-lugal an-ta ed₃-de₃-a-ba*, "after kingship had descended from heaven." The surface rendering is fixed by the central entry `nam-lugal-an-ta-ed-de-a-ba-...` and matches the uniform scholarly consensus (Jacobsen 1939; Glassner 2004; Black et al., ETCSL): *nam-lugal* "kingship" + *an* "heaven/sky" + the ablative *-ta* "from" + *ed₃* "to go down" + the subordinator *-a-ba*.

*an* denotes both the physical sky and the divine sky-realm (and the sky-god An), and *ed₃* is a verb of vertical motion; the Sumerian thus presents kingship as an institution literally *brought down from above*, not merely "instituted." The spatial/physical dimension the Wheel of Heaven apparatus reads in *an-ta* — a descent from the sky — is available in the grammar and is developed in the wiki; it is deliberately NOT imported into the line, which stays at the consensus "from heaven" (accuracy before lens).

Structurally the antediluvian section that follows is the Mesopotamian counterpart to the antediluvian genealogy of Genesis 5 and to the ten pre-Flood kings of Berossus (*Babyloniaca*, 3rd c. BCE; ed. Burstein 1978): a fixed sequence of long-lived figures spanning the interval from the origin of kingship to the Flood (Hallo 1970; R. R. Wilson, *Genealogy and History in the Biblical World*, 1977).

The antediluvian reign-figures — Alulim 28800 years; Alaljar 36000; the dynastic totals 64800, 108000, 241200 — are not random hyperbole but products of the sexagesimal *šár* (3600) and *nēr* (600): 28800 = 8 *šár*, 36000 = 10 *šár*, 43200 = 12 *šár* (Jacobsen 1939). The draft prints the bare composite numeral, matching the ETCSL text and the cuneiform sign-values, with no thousands-separator and no arithmetic gloss; the project-wide convention is recorded at `sexagesimal-reign-figure-rendering-convention-skl`.

The scale is the standard point of contact with the biblical and Berossus antediluvian traditions. Berossus assigns his ten pre-Flood kings 120 *šár* = 432000 years in total (Burstein 1978), and Genesis 5 gives its ten patriarchs life-spans peaking at Methuselah's 969 years — the same "impossibly long antediluvian life" topos rendered in a smaller numerical register (Hallo 1970; cf. Sarna, *Genesis*, JPS, and Cassuto on the Genesis figures).

i18n.en: Dumuzid, the shepherd, ruled for 36000 years.

notes.official:
*Dumuzid* is written with the divine determinative *^d* (DINGIR); per the central `dingir-prefix-prose-drop-convention` the classifier is dropped in the English prose, so the line reads simply "Dumuzid, the shepherd." Here — and for Lugalbanda (107), Gilgameš (112), and the later Ur III / Isin kings written with *^d* (Šulgi and successors) — the determinative marks actual royal *deification*, not merely the orthography of an ordinary divine name; the scope-note `deified-king-dingir-determinative-scope-note-skl` records that the deification is flagged in commentary rather than carried into the prose.

*sipad* "shepherd" is the pastoral-sovereign epithet (see `occupation-epithets-low-born-rulers-skl`). This Dumuzid "the shepherd" of Bad-tibira is distinguished by the list itself from Dumuzid "the fisherman" of Kuara at line 109, and both carry the name of the dying-and-rising god Dumuzid/Tammuz of the central entry.

notes.official:
The Flood enters with *a-ma-ru ba-ur₃*, "the flood swept over." The noun *a-ma-ru* is fixed by the central flood-vocabulary entry (cross-corpus to Akkadian *abūbu* and Hebrew *mabbûl*); the verb *ur₃* means "to sweep, wipe over, efface."

The same collocation closes the antediluvian world in the Sumerian Flood Story (ETCSL 1.7.4, *a-ma-ru … ba-ur₃*), where an explicit object (the cult-centres / the Land) is present; in the King List the verb stands intransitively, with no stated object — the erasure is total and unspecified. This one-line Flood is the composition's structural hinge, dividing the antediluvian dynasties from the post-diluvian exactly as the Deluge divides Genesis 5 from Genesis 10–11 and Berossus's pre- from post-Flood kings.

i18n.en: After the flood had swept over,
and after kingship had descended from heaven,

notes.official: After the Flood the opening formula returns verbatim: kingship *descends from heaven a second time* (see SKL-1). The doubled descent is the composition's ideological spine — kingship is a heavenly institution repeatedly *lowered* to earth, surviving the Flood that erases everything else — and the repetition is deliberate composition, not scribal dittography (Michalowski 1983; Glassner 2004).

Etana, the shepherd, the one who ascended to heaven,

notes.official:
*e-ta-na sipad lu₂ an-še₃ ba-ed₃-de₃*, "Etana, the shepherd, the one who ascended to heaven." The clause is grammatically explicit — *an-še₃* "to heaven" (terminative) + *ed₃* "to go up" — and is governed by the central cross-corpus entry `human-ascent-to-heaven-adapa-etana-enoch-elijah-cross-corpus`, whose `appliesTo` is extended to these lines (see the editor report).

The King List compresses the Old Babylonian Etana Epic, in which the childless shepherd-king is carried up to the heaven of An on the back of an eagle to fetch the "plant of birth" (*šammu ša alādi*) (Kinnier Wilson 1985; Foster, *Before the Muses*, 2005). Etana joins Adapa (summoned before Anu), Enoch (Gen 5:24, "taken"), and Elijah (2 Kgs 2:11, "went up … into heaven") in the cross-corpus motif of the single human lifted bodily into the sky-realm.

The Wheel of Heaven reading of that motif as a literal ascent belongs to the apparatus and the wiki; the line here renders only what the Sumerian states — that Etana went up to heaven.

i18n.en: who made all the lands secure,

notes.official: Several manuscripts (P₃+BT₁₄ and others) insert dynastic-total lines of the form *N mu bal PN-kam*, here "1560 years: the reign of Enmenuna." *bal* is the dynastic "reign, term of office, turn in office" — the very concept of a rotating kingship that structures the whole composition (see `bal-dynastic-reign-term-skl`). These insertion lines (73A, 89A, 106A, 249A, 283A) are treated as translated content — parenthetical dynastic subtotals — rather than demoted to apparatus, following the ETCSL composite's line-numbering.

notes.official:
Meškiaĝgašer is *dumu ^dutu*, "the son of Utu" — Utu the sun-god (Akkadian Šamaš), fixed by the central entry; the *^d* is dropped in prose per convention. His title is *en* (SKL-97, *en-am₃* "was en") paired with *lugal* "king" at 98: the entry `en-lugal-royal-title-distinction-skl` renders standalone *en* as "lord" (ETCSL's range "lord / high priest") and *lugal* as "king," keeping the two Sumerian sovereignty-terms distinct.

*en* is retained untranslated where it is frozen inside the antediluvian throne-names (En-men-lu-ana, En-sipad-zid-ana, Enmebaragesi). The claim that a king is a god's *son* is the Sumerian ideology of divinely-descended kingship, not a biological assertion in the text.

notes.official: Of Meškiaĝgašer the list adds an enigmatic notice with no parallel in the surrounding formulaic entries: he "entered the sea (*ab-ba*) and came up out of it into the mountains (*ḫur-saĝ*)" (SKL-100–101). Whether this records a sea-to-mountain expedition, a disappearance-and-return, or a mythic passage is unrecoverable from the line; the King List preserves it without comment, and so does this translation.

Enam, the king … , ruled for … + 5 years.

notes.official:
*ab-ba-ni lil₂-la₂*, literally "his father (was) a *lil₂*." *lil₂* (Akkadian *lilû*) denotes a wind- or phantom-spirit, a being of the *lilû/lilītu* demon-class; the phrase is a genuine crux, read variously as "a phantom" (ETCSL, "whose father was a phantom(?)"), "a *lila*-spirit," or — taking *lillu* as "deficient one / fool" — "a nobody, a man of no account" (discussed by Jacobsen 1939; George, *The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic*, 2003, notes the competing traditions that make Lugalbanda his father).

The entry `gilgamesh-phantom-father-lil-crux-skl` retains the spirit-reading "a phantom" (claim_type *inferred*, matching ETCSL) without upgrading it to a definite divine or non-human paternity. The hero's semi-divine parentage — elsewhere two-thirds god, son of the goddess Ninsun — is a matter for commentary, and the line renders only the attested crux.

notes.official:
Susuda is *^lu₂azlag₂*, "the fuller" — one of a cluster of occupation-epithets the King List attaches to post-diluvian kings: the boatman (Mamagal, 164), the smith (Meš-He, 126), the leatherworker (Bazi, 215), the fuller again (Zizi, 216), the *gudug*-priest (Limer, 217, a cult-title kept transliterated), the woman tavern-keeper or alewife (Kug-Bau, 225), the stonecutter (Nanniya, 254), and climactically the gardener's son and cupbearer Sargon (267–268). The entry `occupation-epithets-low-born-rulers-skl` renders each with its standard ETCSL value.

The "low-born ruler" motif — kingship passing to men of humble trade — belongs to the composition's ideology that kingship is a mobile, heaven-given office that can alight anywhere, not the property of a bloodline (Michalowski 1983; Marchesi 2010); it culminates in the Sargon legend of the gardener-reared cupbearer who becomes king (cf. the Sargon Birth Legend).

i18n.en: Who was king? Who was not king? {alternate manuscript (in Akkadian): “Who was king? Who was not king?”} {alternate manuscript: “Who was king? Who was king?”}

notes.official:
At the collapse of the dynasty of Agade the list breaks from its ledger-style into a rhetorical couplet, *a-ba-am₃ lugal a-ba-am₃ nu lugal*, "Who was king? Who was not king?" — preserved in one manuscript in Akkadian (*mannum šar mannum lā šar*) and reflecting the anarchy of the Gutian period; a variant reads "Who was king? Who was king?" The couplet is one of the composition's rare departures from the ledger and is rendered directly (see `kingless-interregnum-formulae-skl`).

It pairs with the Gutian notice *lugal mu nu-tuku* (309), "a king who had no name": *mu* is "name" and also "fame, renown," so the phrase carries both "unrecorded" and "unrenowned." Both formulae mark the failure of the King List's central premise — that kingship always rests, nameable, in exactly one city.

notes.official: *suḫuš ki-en-gi-ra mu-un-bu*, "the very foundation of Sumer was torn out," marks the fall of the Ur III dynasty (manuscript P₃+BT₁₄). *ki-en-gi(-r)* is the Sumerians' own name for their land, rendered "Sumer" (`ki-en-gi-sumer-homeland-name-skl`); it is a distinct lexeme from *kalam* / *ka-na-aĝ₂* "the Land" (its own central entry). The King List reaches for the homeland-name here, at the traumatic end of the last great Sumerian dynasty, rather than the generic "Land."

notes.official: The composition closes with its own grand summation: "134 kings (variant 139), … in all" across the "cities in which kingship was exercised." This colophon-like total, treating the whole sequence of dynasties as a single institution of kingship passing from city to city, is the clearest statement of the King List's governing fiction — that at any moment kingship rests in exactly one city, handed on (never shared) down the ages (Jacobsen 1939; Michalowski 1983). The king-count and the surviving year-total are damaged in the manuscripts, and the variants are carried inline.
